title: Show HN: I wrote an entire Vim manual over 4 years
summary: I'm glad to announce that I'm releasing my new book, Learning to Play Vim. When I started using Vim more than a decade ago, I wished there was a manual out there teaching how to use this fantastic editor step by step, beginning with the foundations up to more advanced features. Of course at the time I did the vimtutor, but it was too dense for me to remember much from it. I also read the entire Vim manual (`:help manual`), but I didn't like it: it was too detailed in places (for example `02.8 Finding help` completely lost me for a while), and other features didn't get the treatment they deserved. So I decided to write my own Vim manual. It took me more than 4 years and 2987 focused pomodoros (1244 hours) of work to finally get it done! The result: - 21 chapters showing the most important Vim features step by step. - 170 exercises with solutions. - Many real-life examples to show how Vim can be used and configured for your own needs. - The related Vim's help pages to dig further into each feature. Most configs are both written in Vimscript and Lua for Neovim users. This book explores the common features between Vim and Neovim, so don't expect anything about Neovim-specific features (like treesitter or LSP for example). - The landing page: https://themouseless.dev/vim/ - A sample of the book with the entire table of contents and the first three chapters covering most of the basics: https://themouseless.dev/content/learning_to_play_vim_sample... . I wrote this with my bare hands, no LLM involved to spoil the fun. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50655868 Points: 2 # Comments: 0

title: Show HN: Neui – Go web apps with a built-in AI agent
summary: Neui is an AI agent and a web framework built as one stack. The core is a server-driven Go web framework ( https://github.com/doors-dev/doors ); neui ( https://github.com/doors-dev/neui ) turns each page into an agent harness. FEATURES: The agent sees & operates UI. Annotate what agent can access (links, inputs, buttons), so agent sees it and can assist user with UI operations or even automate it with scripting. ~>neui.Use{ Desc:"submit the form" } Submit or expose context data for the agent: ~neui.Data{Text: "the product shown in the card", Object: product} ... Dynamic tools, right in the markup Same way as you render a button to the user, you give the agent a tool. No endpoints or lifecycle management needed. ~(if user.IsAdmin() { ~neui.Tool[Refund, Receipt]{ Name: "refund", Desc: "Refund the order", Handler: orders.Refund, } }) Work environment Isolated file workspaces and sandboxed scripting ("code mode") out of the box. Agentic apps When a user needs something your UI doesn't have, agent builds it on demand. Complete chat experience Thread list, history, message edits, full-text search, a message queue and automatic compaction. Batteries included MCP connector, web search and .xlsx tools, rich building blocks library for generative apps. COMPARED TO COPILOT KIT: - Agent thread runs on the server, so browser can't rewrite the history/tools to use your LLM backend + less traffic and faster tool-loops - System prompt and provided tool list do not change during operation - it caches and stays hot (because it's usually the same for all your users!) - Pull-based, targeted UI sync; agent monitors only parts of UI that are relevant to the task (compared to full state attached to any user message) - Neui is already a harness with its own sandbox - just bring your model. - For generative UI agent writes a small app on specialized micro framework; agent doesn't need to answer each click or load user input/API responses into context - CON: Is not stack-agnostic, like AG-UI stuff TRY IT: The repo has a demo app with all of this: git clone https://github.com/doors-dev/neui && cd neui DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=... go run ./examples/business-systems/backoffice Then open http://localhost:8095. Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek and any OpenAI-compatible provider will work. STATUS: Both doors and neui are Apache-2.0. I released the first version about 3 weeks ago, so it's early and I am still optimizing some system instructions. Neui itself took me 3 months, on top of the 2 years I spent on the framework underneath (it's awesome, btw), which made it possible. title: Show HN: Graphvein – Trace calls to handlers and tables across repos, no LLM
summary: As I started developing more projects using AI assistance over this year, I started facing the problem that most people have voiced against using AI - the overall architecture/design of the project becomes known only to the agent, and you lose control of the project. I thought what if we could map the architecture, calls, routes, table schemas etc. from the code - that is how this project was born in October. Now I searched a little bit and came upon a few different projects, but none of them did what I wanted to do - at least in full. And quite a few of them used LLMs themselves to do that - which could be plausibly wrong (hallucinated) and non deterministic. Therefore I have built this over the last 2 months to create a base which: 1. Extracts routes, table schema, request and response bodies across HTTP requests, Tauri calls etc. 2. Gives you an overview of the architecture which you can dive into including how each handler is linked to routes or tables - it works in both directions in a fan out mode from any layer 3. Gives you an overview of the table schema extracted from the project and how they link together 4. An OpenAPI spec extracted from the project, with a try-it mode like Swagger 5. Change impact and what changing a particular piece of code might impact across the stack 6. It supports zero or more frontends, and one or more backends together in a project and how they all link together It supports TypeScript / JavaScript (Express, Next.js, Angular, Angular HttpClient, hey-api, fetch, axios, Prisma, Drizzle, Sequelize, TypeORM, Orval and Supabase clients), Python (FastAPI, SQLModel), Go (net/http, chi, gin, GORM), and Rust (Axum, Tauri commands, Diesel). Database support is for SQL (tested with Postgres) and Java, C# and Dart get structure only in this preview release. It also has a read-only MCP server which agents can use to get Graphvein-verified information and not have to grep around files to figure things out. No data leaves your computer (other than the try it environments you configure yourself), and everything is done locally, without any LLM (not even local LLMs). I do plan on adding LLM support in the future, but only building upon this base - for gap-filling, generation of wikis and other features which can use the deterministic core and build upon it. And it will remain opt-in even then. Please feel free to check out the GitHub repo or the website ( https://graphvein.com/ ) to get more details. Please let me know which language support/framework would make this more appealing to use, or if you have any other feature requests. title: Show HN: Sandbox platform on Kubernetes for secure remote access without secrets
summary: Cordium is a FOSS, self-hosted, identity-based, general-purpose sandbox platform built on Kubernetes. The primary differentiator here is that Cordium automatically assigns an identity to each sandbox to provide "secretless" secure zero-trust remote access to resources/infrastructure (e.g. APIs, SSH, databases, k8s, etc.) without having to hold credentials and secrets (e.g. API keys and access tokens, SSH private keys/passwords, database passwords, mTLS private keys, etc.) inside the sandbox. The way it works is that every Cordium sandbox includes an Octelium ZTNA client (see https://github.com/octelium/octelium ) which routes requests from the sandbox to the upstream resources through the Octelium Cluster running on the same underlying Kubernetes cluster over WireGuard tunnels. In the Octelium Cluster, each upstream resource is protected by a corresponding identity-aware proxy that actually holds the upstream credential that injects the credential on-the-fly to the upstream if the downstream (i.e. the Cordium sandbox) is authorized by an Octelium policy. In short, Cordium is basically a sandbox platform with a _dual nature_: it doesn't just provide isolated execution runtimes but it also provides and identity and access infrastructure to provide secure secretless remote access, identity management, L7-aware access control and visibility for every request originating from within the sandbox. You can use it for various use cases from a personal self-hosted GitHub Codespaces alternative for remote development as well as a scalable sandbox platform for AI agents to access infrastructure without handling them your credentials at scale. You can also use it as an infrastructure layer to build more complex applications such as agent meshes. The primary features include declarative management, Templates and prebuilds, persistent, ephemeral and forkable storage via Kubernetes volume snapshots, lifecycle tasks, controls such as linux caps, read-only filesystem and egress control, access and management over web portal/SSH/CLI as well as SDKs in Go/Rust/Python/Typescript. You can learn more about Cordium, its features in detail and how it works, please visit the docs at https://octelium.com/docs/cordium/latest/overview/intro You can also try a live demo for the Cordium web portal at https://demo.octelium.com/cordium and a CLI playground at https://demo.octelium.com/cli Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50660739 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

title: Show HN: SimDrop – Running iOS simulators in the macOS Finder sidebar
summary: Hi HN, I made a small macOS utility for my own iOS simulator workflow. I kept running into two annoyances: getting config files in and out of a simulator is clunky (digging into CoreSimulator UUID folders or running simctl), and on the iPhone Duo simulator I couldn't even drag and drop images onto the window at all. SimDrop puts every running iOS simulator in Finder's sidebar (under Locations) with two folders: - Downloads/ (Files app > On My iPhone > Downloads) - Photos and Videos/ (the simulator's Photos library) Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when they shut down. Everything is also reachable from the terminal under ~/Library/CloudStorage/SimDrop-SimDrop/. A couple of caveats up front: - Dragging moves files by default (same as iCloud Drive, because it uses File Provider on the startup volume)—hold Option to copy. - macOS 15+ and iOS simulators only (not physical devices). It's free, open source (GPL-3.0), signed and notarized, and installable via Homebrew: brew install --cask rxliuli/tap/sim-drop Just sharing in case others run into the same friction—feedback or PRs welcome! summary: I started working on this around a year ago because of my frustration with the norm in tech - where everything is tracked and you pay rent while owning none of it. It began as a private, low-effort way for neurodivergent people to take notes and put almost anything on a canvas. It’s since grown into a whole peer-to-peer workspace. I may have subscriptions in the future for people who want integrations with centralised apps and cloud convenience but you can use Hubris fully without it. summary: Do you run multiple AI agents in terminals, in bots, concurrently remotely and locally? There's virtually no setup; just point your agents at the website, they install StatusPan and start pushing notification to it. If you're working on one machine, that's all you need. title: Show HN: I posted a read-later-to-paper app here in 2020. Here's what happened
summary: Six years ago I posted "Turn your read later folder into a physical book" here ( https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=24690310 ) and went to watch a movie. I’ve been lurking in HN but didn’t really think much of it. Soon enough, people put all sorts of articles in our engine, commenting in the thread, sharing stories. I was definitely not prepared for this. The idea seemed to resonate, or at least the problem did, so we got excited and built the full thing. And when we eventually launched, people ordered books and seemed to enjoy the reading experience, but it quickly became clear this wasn't going to turn into a habit. It was aspirational, maybe cool, but it didn’t solve the actual problem, which is when you decide you want to read something properly, you need to get off the feed. So lots of books have been in bedside tables instead of reading later folders, as the intent didn’t match the delivery. The people who stuck around actually used it as a print button - curating reading experiences and when they wanted to invest time in reading, printed at home (or at staples) and did just that. But Screenbreak wasn’t getting any meaningful traction, so we put it on autopilot and focused on other things. But when AI came around, I started thinking more about what we should build now that we weren’t able back then, and what we would do differently knowing what we'd learned? The first thing I wanted to check is how good our engine could become with minimal effort. Our latest version on Zyte's article extraction benchmark ( https://github.com/scrapinghub/article-extraction-benchmark ), scored 0.896 (not bad). So we split the benchmark in half and tuned our engine in one half, and it reached 0.96 for this half. But on the other half, it scored 0.924, so there was a bit more work to do to reach readability (0.947) or trafilatura (0.958). But we knew extraction was half of the struggle. The other half is typesetting. How you handle images, captions, tables and page breaks, across different designs. And with AI allowing us to work with Javascript more, we ported our typesetting rules and rebuilt the extraction engine around Mozilla's Readability, so it could run in your browser, and get those speed gains as well, on top of a higher baseline. With our extraction rules around it, we're at 0.957 (almost as trafilatura), and the typesetting rules sit on top of that. With that working, we started thinking about what the product should actually be this time around. And we decided to focus on the simplest action, what we wanna call the print button of the web. No account, free, instantly accessible. But we also knew a big part of the pain was the read later folders sitting there. So instead of building new workflows, we tried to build as simply as possible around existing workflows. Import the bookmarks that matter from your browser or send your newsletters directly. And as the pile grows longer, maybe use your agent to sift through it and propose a reading experience by asking ”build a 45’ booklet of good science reading”. And if e-ink is your thing, you can send it to your Kindle. We haven’t gone back full time, but it's a fun way to keep building on the side with speed :) Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50656884 Points: 2 # Comments: 0

title: Show HN: Yioop 10 – a PHP search engine that runs groups, wikis, Git and mail
summary: Yioop is an open source (GPLv3) search engine written in PHP that I have been working on since 2009. Version 10 is now out. Yioop comes with a crawler which can be used on the open web or on a list of sites you choose. It can also index Wikipedia XML dumps, arc and warc archives, Open Directory RDF, and dumps of email or databases, and several crawls can be mixed into one set of results. A media updater re-indexes RSS and Atom feeds every hour, so news makes it into the results. Besides search, Yioop can be used to run discussion groups, blogs and wikis. Each group has a wiki for pages, slide presentations and spreadsheets, and the wiki can be used to build whole web sites. Some of what is new in version 10: - Yioop can run on its own Pure PHP web server, with HTTPS, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 support, and has its own web configurable PHP mail server and client. - Users can make voice and video calls from their messages. - Common audio and video formats are decoded and encoded in Yioop's own PHP code. - A wiki page can hold a git repository that people clone and push to over HTTP, with an issue tracker beside it. - Yioop is available in 25 languages, and a faster tokenizer handles text in each of them, including Chinese, Japanese and Korean. Yioop's stemmers, summarizers and other language tools can also be used in other projects through Composer.
